subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10! In this unit you will master one of the most useful tools in all of mathematics: the percentage. Percentages are everywhere in daily life. When Amina sees a market stall in Hargeisa advertising 25% off on fabric, when Yusuf reads that a football striker has a 75% shot-accuracy record, or when Hassan's family works out how much sadaqah to give from the month's savings, they are all thinking in percentages. Learning to handle them confidently will help you make smart decisions with money, understand the news, and read data like an expert.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Recognise percentages of shapes and whole numbers, including percentages less than 1 or greater than 100.
Recognise that fractions, terminating decimals and percentages have equivalent values.
Estimate, multiply and divide proper fractions.
Estimate, multiply and divide decimals by whole numbers.
Understand and explain that probabilities range from 0 to 1, and can be represented as proper fractions, decimals and percentages.
Use knowledge of place value to multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by any positive power of 10.

outcomes: Explain what a percentage means as a number of parts out of 100.
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages in both directions.
Recall common equivalents such as 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% without stopping to calculate.
Find a percentage of a quantity using the decimal method, the fraction method and mental strategies, including percentages that are less than 1% (such as 0.5%) or greater than 100%.
Work out a percentage increase or decrease and apply it using a multiplier.
Calculate the percentage change between an original value and a new value.
Solve reverse percentage problems to find an original amount.
Handle compound percentage changes applied one after another.
Interpret percentage information in real situations and spot when it might be misleading.

concepts.title: What a Percentage Really Means
concepts.explanation:
A percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100. The symbol % means “out of 100.” So when you read 25%, you should hear in your head “25 out of every 100,” which is the fraction 25/100. Picture a large square grid divided into 100 tiny squares, like a wall of 100 small tiles in the market. If 25 of those tiles are painted blue, then 25% of the wall is blue. This picture – the hundred grid – is worth keeping in your mind throughout the unit.

Why are percentages so useful? Because they give us a fair way to compare things that start from different totals. Suppose one class has 8 out of 20 students who walk to school, and another class has 12 out of 30. At first glance the numbers 8 and 12 look different, so it is hard to say which class walks more. But convert each to a percentage: 8 out of 20 is 40%, and 12 out of 30 is also 40%. Now we can see instantly that the two classes are exactly the same in proportion, even though the actual numbers differ. Percentages act like a common language that lets us compare fairly.

Percentages are not limited to the range 0 to 100. A percentage can be greater than 100%. If a young mango tree grows from 20 cm to 50 cm, its new height is 250% of its original height, because 50 is two-and-a-half times 20. If a trader's profit rises from 100,000 shillings to 150,000 shillings, the new profit is 150% of the old profit. A percentage over 100% simply means “more than the whole original amount.”
concepts.example: Percentages can also be smaller than 1%. These tiny percentages appear in science and in careful measurement. The concentration of salt in a weak solution might be 0.5%, and the chance of a rare event might be 0.01%. A percentage less than 1% just means “less than one part in a hundred.” Do not let very large or very small percentages confuse you – the meaning is always the same: a number of parts out of 100.

concepts.title: Converting Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
concepts.explanation: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three different costumes worn by the same idea – a part of a whole. A confident mathematician can change any one form into the others without hesitation. Let us learn each direction carefully. To turn a fraction into a percentage, multiply by 100%. For example, 1/4 × 100% = 25%, and 3/5 × 100% = 60%, and 7/8 × 100% = 87.5%. A quick way to think about it: find an equivalent fraction with 100 on the bottom, and the top number is your percentage. Since 1/4 is the same as 25/100, it is 25%.
concepts.example: To turn a decimal into a percentage, again multiply by 100. So 0.25 becomes 25%, 0.6 becomes 60%, and 0.875 becomes 87.5%. A handy shortcut is that multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the right. Be careful with this shortcut, though: 0.6 is 60%, not 6%. Whenever you are unsure, go back to the rule “multiply by 100” and you will not slip.

concepts.title: Finding a Percentage of a Quantity
concepts.explanation: One of the most common tasks is finding a percentage of an amount — for instance, 30% of 80 goats, or 15% of a 40-shilling bill. There are three reliable methods, and it is smart to know all three so you can pick the easiest one for each problem. Change the percentage into a decimal, then multiply. To find 30% of 80, write 30% as 0.30 and calculate 0.30 × 80 = 24. This method is quick with a calculator and works for any numbers. Percentages smaller than 1% work exactly the same way; they just need extra care with the decimal point. A percentage less than 1% is written with a decimal in front of the % sign, such as 0.5% or 0.25%. To find 0.5% of an amount, first write it as a decimal: 0.5% = 0.5 ÷ 100 = 0.005. Then multiply as usual.
concepts.example: Change the percentage into a fraction, then multiply. To find 30% of 80, write 30% as 30/100 = 3/10, then 3/10 × 80 = 240/10 = 24. This method shines when the fraction is simple, such as 50% (a half) or 25% (a quarter). For example, 0.5% of 4,000 shillings is 0.005 × 4,000 = 20 shillings. It helps to check the size of your answer: since 0.5% is half of 1%, and 1% of 4,000 is 40, half of that is 20 — which matches, so the answer is sensible.

concepts.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
concepts.explanation:
Often we do not just want a percentage of an amount – we want to change an amount by a percentage. Prices rise, populations grow, and savings earn interest. The neat way to do this is with a multiplier, a single decimal you multiply by.

To increase a number by a percentage, multiply by (100% + the percentage), written as a decimal. To increase 50 by 20%, the multiplier is 100% + 20% = 120% = 1.20, so the new amount is 50 × 1.20 = 60. The whole original is the 100%, and the extra 20% is added on, giving 120% of the original in total.

To decrease a number by a percentage, multiply by (100% − the percentage). To decrease 80 by 15%, the multiplier is 100% − 15% = 85% = 0.85, so the new amount is 80 × 0.85 = 68. You are keeping 85% of the original and losing 15%.

The multiplier method is faster and safer than the older two-step way of “find the percentage, then add or subtract.” Once you can see that a 20% rise means × 1.20 and a 15% fall means × 0.85, a huge range of problems becomes one-line calculations. Here is a small table of common multipliers to lock into memory: a 10% rise is × 1.10; a 5% rise is × 1.05; a 25% fall is × 0.75; a 30% fall is × 0.70; and a 100% rise (doubling) is × 2.00.
concepts.example: Let us see the multiplier at work in a real setting. Ibrahim keeps 40 goats. This year his herd grows by 15%. The multiplier for a 15% increase is 1.15, so his new herd is 40 × 1.15 = 46 goats. Now suppose a drought the following year reduces the herd by 25%. The multiplier for a 25% decrease is 0.75, so 46 × 0.75 = 34.5, which we round to 34 goats since we cannot have half a goat. Notice how each change starts from the most recent amount, not the original – a key idea we return to later in the unit.

concepts.title: Calculating the Percentage Change
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes we know the old value and the new value, and we want to know by what percentage it changed. This is the percentage change, and it has one clear formula that you should learn by heart:

Percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100%

The result tells you two things at once. If it is positive, the value went up, and the size of the number is the percentage increase. If it is negative, the value went down, and the size of the number is the percentage decrease. The single most important rule is that you always divide by the original value – the amount you started from – never the new one.

Here is a worked increase. A population grows from 50,000 to 55,000. The change is 55,000 − 50,000 = 5,000. Divide by the original: 5,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.1. Multiply by 100%: 10% increase. And a worked decrease: a price drops from 80 to 60. The change is 60 − 80 = −20. Divide by the original: −20 ÷ 80 = −0.25. Multiply by 100%: −25%, which we describe as a 25% decrease.
concepts.example: Watch out for a common trap: the percentage change is not symmetric. Going from 80 down to 60 is a 25% decrease, but going from 60 back up to 80 is a 33.3% increase, because the original value has changed. The direction matters, and so does which number you treat as the starting point. Whenever Zahra calculates a percentage change, she pauses and asks herself one question first: “What was the original amount here?” That single habit prevents most errors.

concepts.title: Reverse Percentage Problems
concepts.explanation:
A reverse percentage problem gives you the amount after a change and asks for the amount before it. These feel harder at first, but the multiplier makes them straightforward: since multiplying by the multiplier goes forwards, dividing by the multiplier goes backwards.

Consider this: after a 20% pay rise, Omar's monthly wage is now 36,000 shillings. What was it before? The rise means the new wage is 120% of the old, so the multiplier is 1.20. To reverse it, divide: 36,000 ÷ 1.20 = 30,000 shillings. We can check by working forwards: 30,000 × 1.20 = 36,000. It matches, so we are right.

Now a decrease example. After a 15% discount, a jacket costs 68 shillings. What was the original price? A 15% discount means the sale price is 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85. Reverse it by dividing: 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80 shillings. Check forwards: 80 × 0.85 = 68. Correct.
concepts.example: The single biggest mistake in reverse problems is to take the percentage of the wrong amount. It is tempting to think “15% of 68” and add it back, but that is wrong, because the 15% was taken from the original 80, not from the sale price of 68. The safe approach every time is: decide what percentage the given amount represents, express that as a multiplier, and divide. To solve any reverse problem, follow four steps: identify what you know and what you need, decide what percentage the known amount is of the original, write the equation using the multiplier, and divide to find the original – then check by working forwards.

methods.title: How to find a percentage of an amount
methods.example: Express 7/20 as a decimal and a percentage.
steps: Change the percentage to a decimal by dividing by 100.
Multiply the decimal by the amount.
Check with a mental estimate built from 10% and 1%.

methods.title: How to work out a percentage change
methods.example: A school has 480 students. 35% are in Year 7. How many Year 7 students are there?
steps: Subtract the original from the new value to get the change.
Divide the change by the original amount.
Multiply by 100% and state whether it is an increase or a decrease.

methods.title: How to solve a reverse percentage problem
methods.example: A salary of 45,000 shillings increases by 8%. What is the new salary?
steps: Decide what percentage of the original the given amount represents.
Write this as a multiplier (for example 120% = 1.20).
Divide the given amount by the multiplier to find the original.
Check by working forwards again.

methods.title: Percentage decrease with a multiplier
methods.example: A car worth 18,000 shillings loses 15% of its value. What is it now worth?
steps: The multiplier for a 15% decrease is 100% − 15% = 85% = 0.85.
So the value is 18,000 × 0.85 = 15,300 shillings.
Check by finding 15% of 18,000 and subtracting it from 18,000 — you should get the same answer, 15,300.

methods.title: Calculate a percentage change
methods.example: A stock price rises from 25 to 32. Find the percentage increase.
steps: Change = 32 − 25 = 7.
Divide by the original: 7 ÷ 25 = 0.28.
Multiply by 100%: 28% increase.
We divided by 25, the original value, not by 32.

methods.title: A reverse percentage problem
methods.example: After a 30% discount, a jacket costs 84 shillings. What was the original price?
steps: A 30% discount means the sale price is 70% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.70.
Divide to reverse: 84 ÷ 0.70 = 120 shillings.
Check forwards: 120 × 0.70 = 84.
Correct.

workedExamples.title: Convert a fraction to a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: Express 7/20 as a decimal and a percentage.
workedExamples.solution: Make the denominator 100 by multiplying top and bottom by 5: 7/20 = 35/100. So 7/20 = 0.35 = 35%. As a check, 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35, and 0.35 × 100 = 35%.

workedExamples.title: Find a percentage of a quantity
workedExamples.prompt: A school has 480 students. 35% are in Year 7. How many Year 7 students are there?
workedExamples.solution: Use the decimal method: 35% = 0.35, so 0.35 × 480 = 168 students. Mental check: 10% of 480 is 48, so 30% is 144; 5% is 24; 144 + 24 = 168. The two methods agree.

workedExamples.title: Percentage increase with a multiplier
workedExamples.prompt: A salary of 45,000 shillings increases by 8%. What is the new salary?
workedExamples.solution: The multiplier for an 8% increase is 100% + 8% = 108% = 1.08. So the new salary is 45,000 × 1.08 = 48,600 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Percentage decrease with a multiplier
workedExamples.prompt: A car worth 18,000 shillings loses 15% of its value. What is it now worth?
workedExamples.solution: The multiplier for a 15% decrease is 100% − 15% = 85% = 0.85. So the value is 18,000 × 0.85 = 15,300 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Calculate a percentage change
workedExamples.prompt: A stock price rises from 25 to 32. Find the percentage increase.
workedExamples.solution: Change = 32 − 25 = 7. Divide by the original: 7 ÷ 25 = 0.28. Multiply by 100%: 28% increase. We divided by 25, the original value, not by 32.

workedExamples.title: A reverse percentage problem
workedExamples.prompt: After a 30% discount, a jacket costs 84 shillings. What was the original price?
workedExamples.solution: A 30% discount means the sale price is 70% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.70. Divide to reverse: 84 ÷ 0.70 = 120 shillings. Check forwards: 120 × 0.70 = 84. Correct.

workedExamples.title: A compound change
workedExamples.prompt: A value increases by 20%, then decreases by 10%. What is the overall percentage change?
workedExamples.solution: Combine the multipliers: 1.20 × 0.90 = 1.08. That is a multiplier of 1.08, which means an 8% increase overall. Adding 20% and −10% to get 10% would be wrong, because the second change acts on a larger amount.

workedExamples.title: A reverse compound problem
workedExamples.prompt: A computer's price drops 20% in one month, then a further 15% the next month. The final price is 680 shillings. What was the original price?
workedExamples.solution: The combined multiplier is 0.80 × 0.85 = 0.68. To reverse, divide: 680 ÷ 0.68 = 1,000 shillings. Check forwards: 1,000 × 0.80 = 800, then 800 × 0.85 = 680. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Find the percentage change
workedExamples.prompt: Find the percentage change: a) 40 to 50 b) 80 to 64 c) 25 to 32.
workedExamples.solution: a) 25% increase, b) 20% decrease, c) 28% increase.

activities.title: The Hundred Grid
steps: Draw a 10 by 10 grid, giving 100 small squares.
Shade 25 squares in one colour and 40 squares in another.
Write the percentage each colour represents, and the fraction and decimal too.
Ask a family member (or your AI tutor, if no one is available) to name a percentage and shade exactly that many squares.
The hundred grid makes it easy to see that a percentage is simply a number of parts out of 100.

activities.title: Market Discount Hunt
activities.materials: real or pretend prices (write price tags for household items).
steps: Give each item a price in shillings.
Choose a discount for each: 10%, 25% or 50%.
Work out the saving and the sale price using a multiplier.
Compare two offers on the same item and decide which is the better deal.
This trains you to find discounts quickly – a skill you will use in every market for the rest of your life.

activities.title: The Percentage Card Game
activities.materials: cards showing fractions, decimals and percentages that match (for example 1/2, 0.5, 50%).
steps: Make sets of three matching cards (fraction, decimal, percentage).
Shuffle all the cards and deal them out.
Take turns laying down cards and claiming a matching set of three.
The player with the most complete sets wins.
Playing this a few times will make the common equivalents automatic.

activities.title: The Savings Investigation
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a calculator if you have one.
steps: Imagine saving 1,000 shillings that grows by 5% each year.
Work out the amount after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years using the multiplier 1.05.
Record the results in a table and describe how the growth changes.
Investigate: how many years until the savings first pass 1,300 shillings?
This investigation shows the surprising power of compound growth over time.

activities.title: Percentages in the News (Family Task)
activities.materials: a newspaper, radio report, or a story an adult can share.
steps: Find a statement that uses a percentage, such as a price rise or a survey result.
Discuss with your family, or your AI tutor if no one is available, what the percentage really means.
Check whether the statement could be misleading – what is the total it is based on?
Write one sentence explaining the percentage clearly in your own words.
This helps you become a careful reader of the percentages that fill the news every day.

activities.title: Fair Shares and Sadaqah
activities.materials: a small amount of pretend money in shillings (paper coins).
steps: Imagine a family saves 8,000 shillings in a month.
Work out 10% of it to give as sadaqah (charity), which can be any amount the giver chooses.
Work out how much remains after giving.
Try again with a different saving amount and a different percentage.
This links percentages to sharing and generosity, showing how the maths supports thoughtful decisions.

realProblems.prompt: At an Eastleigh market, a jacket is priced at 150 shillings. Sahra has a 20% off voucher. a) What is the discounted price? b) If sales tax of 6.5% is then added, what does she pay? c) If she had waited for a 35% sale instead, how much more would she have saved than with the voucher?
realProblems.answer: a) 150 × 0.80 = 120; b) 120 × 1.065 = 127.80; c) the voucher saves 150 − 120 = 30, while a 35% sale gives 150 × 0.65 = 97.50 and saves 150 − 97.50 = 52.50, so the sale saves 22.50 more.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Percentage, Multiplier, Percentage increase / decrease), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.

selfAssessment: I can explain what a percentage means as a number of parts out of 100.
I can convert between fractions, decimals and percentages in both directions.
I can recall common equivalents such as 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% without stopping to calculate.
I can find a percentage of a quantity using the decimal method, the fraction method and mental strategies, including percentages that are less than 1% (such as 0.5%) or greater than 100%.
I can work out a percentage increase or decrease and apply it using a multiplier.
I can calculate the percentage change between an original value and a new value.
I can solve reverse percentage problems to find an original amount.
I can handle compound percentage changes applied one after another.
I can interpret percentage information in real situations and spot when it might be misleading.
